catalog_quote: Torero (1964: 461-462), que ofrece una discusión provisional de este aspecto de la prosodia quechua, sugiere que el régimen acentual proporcionado por el dominico pudo haber sido tal vez el del PQ. Entre los dialectos quechuas que ofrecen un patrón acentual reminiscente del descrito por el gramático mencionado figuran, según Torero, el ancashino (cf., en efecto, Parker 1967) y las hablas de Cajatambo y Chancay (Lima); a ellos pueden agregarse también las variedades de Ferreñafe (Escribens 1977: 50-53) y Amazonas (Taylor 1975: 36-37). En éstas la carga culminativa depende de la posición y del carácter constitutivo de las sílabas dentro de la palabra. De esta manera, lo que distingue a tales dialectos de los demás es que en ellos la sílaba inicial puede portar el rasgo culminativo, si reúne las condiciones: hecho inusitado en el resto de las variedades en donde prima la acentuación penúltima. [ch. VIII, Google Books snippet:] ... primera sílaba con un acento secundario que recae en la penúltima, cuando la palabra contiene más de tres sílabas. Tales dialectos, entre los que caben mencionar a las hablas de Cajatambo y Chancay (Lima), Ancash, Ferreñafe (Lambayeque) y ... [Adelaar & Muysken 2004: 207, snippet:] ... stress is predominant. More complex, non-penultimate stress patterns, involving word-initial stress and stress dependent on syllable structure, are found in QI Ancash and in QI Cajatambo (cf. Torero 1964: 461; Parker 1976) ...

new_statements.quote: ...dialectos quechuas que ofrecen un patrón acentual reminiscente del descrito por el gramático mencionado figuran, según Torero, el ancashino (cf., en efecto, Parker 1967) y las hablas de Cajatambo y Chancay (Lima); a ellos pueden agregarse también las variedades de Ferreñafe (Escribens 1977: 50-53) y Amazonas (Taylor 1975: 36-37). En éstas la carga culminativa depende de la posición y del carácter constitutivo de las sílabas dentro de la palabra. De esta manera, lo que distingue a tales dialectos de los demás es que en ellos la sílaba inicial puede portar el rasgo culminativo, si reúne las condiciones: hecho inusitado en el resto de las variedades en donde prima la acentuación penúltima.
new_statements.translation: ...Quechua dialects showing an accentual pattern reminiscent of the one described by the aforementioned grammarian [Domingo de Santo Tomás] include, according to Torero, Ancash Quechua (cf. indeed Parker 1967) and the varieties of Cajatambo and Chancay (Lima); to these may be added Ferreñafe (Escribens 1977: 50-53) and Amazonas (Taylor 1975: 36-37). In these the culminative (stress) load depends on the position and on the make-up of the syllables within the word. Thus what sets these dialects apart from the rest is that in them the initial syllable can carry the culminative feature, if it meets the conditions — something unheard-of in the other varieties, where penultimate accentuation prevails.
new_statements.citation: Cerrón-Palomino, Rodolfo. 1987. Lingüística quechua. Cusco: Centro de Estudios Rurales Andinos 'Bartolomé de Las Casas', cap. IV sec. 4.5 (el acento); reporting Torero 1964:461. Corroborated by Adelaar & Muysken 2004:207.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Unlike general Quechua penultimate stress, Cajatambo (with Chancay/Huaral and Ancash) has stress placement conditioned by syllable position and syllable structure (weight), such that the word-initial syllable may take primary stress when the conditions are met; Adelaar & Muysken 2004:207 gloss the same facts as 'word-initial stress and stress dependent on syllable structure.. in quantity-insensitive Ancash and in quantity-insensitive Cajatambo (cf. Torero 1964: 461)'. The explicit conditions are not given in the accessible text; the Ancash analogue (Parker 1976:58-59) is: stress the non-final heavy (closed or long-vowel) syllable, otherwise the initial syllable, in clause-final/citation forms.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Cerrón-Palomino's dialectology chapter (snippet, gbfeed_cp1987_o/): '..primera sílaba con un acento secundario que recae en la penúltima, cuando la palabra contiene más de tres sílabas. Tales dialectos, entre los que caben mencionar a las hablas de Cajatambo y Chancay (Lima), Ancash, Ferreñafe (Lambayeque) y..' — i.e. primary stress on the first syllable with a secondary stress on the penult in words of more than three syllables (the words immediately preceding 'primera sílaba' fall in a snippet gap).
new_statements.exceptions: None visible for Cajatambo specifically; the general-Quechua statement in the same passage is 'el acento de intensidad recae sobre la penúltima sílaba de la palabra' with these dialects as the exception. Parker 1976 (Ancash analogue) notes final stress in interjections and on word-final long syllables (1st-person length).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level culminative stress; Cerrón-Palomino speaks of 'la palabra'. Parker's Ancash description, which both secondary sources pair with Cajatambo, distinguishes clause-final (incl. citation) forms from clause-medial forms; whether Torero 1964 makes the same distinction for Cajatambo could not be checked.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statements concern 'las hablas de Cajatambo' = the Quechua of Cajatambo province (upper Pativilca, dept. Lima), i.e. caja1239 / ISO qvl proper; Cerrón-Palomino groups it with Chancay (Huaral province, North Lima; Glottolog chan1318-area varieties) and Ancash-Huaylas (huay1240). Note Glottolog/UNESCO alt-names for caja1239 ('Yaru, Tarma, Junín') reflect a broader 'Cajatambo–Pasco–N Junín' lumping; the accent statement applies to Cajatambo province speech only, not to Yaru/Tarma. Pacaraos (paca1245), also North Lima, has a different, partly phonemic stress system and is not covered by this statement.

new_statements.quote: Otherwise, penultimate stress is predominant. More complex, non-penultimate stress patterns, involving word-initial stress and stress dependent on syllable structure, are found in QI Ancash and in QI Cajatambo (cf. Torero 1964: 461; Parker 1976). The northern Peruvian dialects QUIA Ferreñafe (Escribens 1977) and QIIB Amazonas (Taylor 1975; Chaparro 1985)

new_statements.relation_note: Same type as the existing statement (Cerrón-Palomino 1987 sec. 4.5, reporting Torero 1964: 461-462): non-penultimate, initial stress possible, placement dependent on syllable structure = weight-sensitive. It adds no rule detail and lumps quantity-insensitive Cajatambo with quantity-insensitive Ancash. The full book is lending-restricted on archive.org ( could not be reached by automated download) and the WALS refdb URL is a bibliographic record, so the sentence was reconstructed verbatim from overlapping archive.org full-text-search highlights, which agree word for word with the independent Google Books snippet of p. 207.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Against the Quechuan default of penultimate stress, Cajatambo (with Ancash) has a non-penultimate pattern: stress can be word-initial and its position depends on syllable structure (weight). No explicit rule for Cajatambo itself is given; the statement is second-hand, citing Torero 1964: 461 and Parker 1976.
new_statements.secondary_stress: not mentioned in the recovered passage
new_statements.exceptions: The preceding sentence (only partly recovered: '.. first-person marker -y. Otherwise, penultimate stress is predominant.') treats the final-stressed first-person forms as the general Quechuan exception; nothing Cajatambo-specific.
new_statements.identity_note: Adelaar & Muysken 2004 label the variety 'quantity-insensitive Cajatambo' (Quechua I, Cajatambo province, Lima) and group it with quantity-insensitive Ancash for stress. Solís Fonseca 2002 describes the Quechua of southern Ancash (Bolognesi province) across the Pativilca river, where it identifies 'elementos quechuas tipo Cajatambo', but it is not a description of Cajatambo Quechua itself and says nothing about stress. The catalog record for caja1239 currently has an empty rule field; the only rule-bearing statement remains Cerrón-Palomino 1987 (weight-sensitive) and Adelaar & Muysken 2004 now corroborates it.

new_statements.quote: More complex, non-penultimate stress patterns, involving word-initial stress and stress dependent on syllable structure, are found in QI Ancash and in QI Cajatambo (cf. Torero 1964: 461; Parker 1976). The northern Peruvian dialects QIIA Ferreñafe (Escribens 1977) and QIIB Amazonas (Taylor 1975; Chaparro 1985) also have deviant stress patterns, as had the sixteenth-century coastal dialect described by Santo Tomás. For the dialect of Huaraz (department of Ancash) the following stress pattern is described (Torero 1964). Syllables can be either long (CVC, CV:) or short (CV). If a word contains a long syllable which is not word-final, the latter is stressed.

new_statements.relation_note: Same type as the catalog record (weight-hedged, from Cerrón-Palomino 1987 sec. 4.5 reporting Torero 1964:461-462) and word-for-word identical to existing statement no. 2, which had been reconstructed from archive.org full-text-search and Google Books snippets: the full text confirms that reconstruction verbatim and its page (207). Adds no Cajatambo-specific rule beyond 'word-initial stress and stress dependent on syllable structure'; the detailed weight rule is attributed to Huaraz (Ancash). All statements held by the project trace to one primary source, Torero 1964:461.
new_statements.rule_in_words: General Quechua: stress on the penultimate vowel of every polysyllabic word (p.206). quantity-insensitive Cajatambo is named, together with quantity-insensitive Ancash, as an exception with non-penultimate stress: word-initial stress occurs and placement depends on syllable structure (long = CVC or CV: vs short = CV), citing Torero 1964:461 and Parker 1976. The explicit weight rule that follows (a non-final long syllable is stressed; with several, the last or the long-vowel one, or stress spread; with none, the first syllable, or the final if it has a long vowel) is stated for Huaraz (Ancash), not spelled out separately for Cajatambo; the book gives no Cajatambo data of its own.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing on secondary stress for Cajatambo; for Huaraz it notes stress 'can be distributed over several long syllables'.
new_statements.exceptions: Pan-Quechua: word-final stress in interjections/emphatic expressions (alaláw) and, in quantity-insensitive, on a word-final first-person long-vowel morpheme (wasí-: 'my house'); footnote 24: whether the Ancash-type pattern reflects Proto-Quechua (Torero 1964) is debated, the authors favour inherited penultimate stress.
new_statements.identity_note: 'quantity-insensitive Cajatambo' = the Quechua I (Central Quechua) speech of the province of Cajatambo (dept. Lima), grouped by the authors with quantity-insensitive Ancash (Huaylas-Conchucos) for stress; the book treats it in the general Quechua phonology section (3.2.5), with no separate sketch or data.

tone_statements.citation: Valqui, Jairo. 2018. El acento en el quechua de Chachapoyas: un sustrato de la lengua chacha o un vestigio protoquechua [Stress in Chachapoyas Quechua: a linguistic stratum of the Chacha language or a Proto-Quechua vestige]. Letras (Lima) 89(130): 79-99.
tone_statements.quote: En Cajatambo, de acuerdo con los datos proporcionados por Carreño (2010), el acento regularmente recae en la primera sílaba tanto en nombres como en verbos. Según el citado autor, “el acento cajatambino es un acento fijo y de tonalidad, que se coloca, siempre y solamente, en la primera sílaba de la palabra” (Carreño, 2010, p. 54). … Lo más curioso es su realización fonética; es un acento tonal, que consiste en una ligera elevación en el tono de la voz que acompaña al inicio de cada palabra. Esa continua sucesión de elevaciones del tono, que se da en toda frase quechua …
tone_statements.translation: In Cajatambo, according to the data provided by Carreño (2010), the accent regularly falls on the first syllable in nouns as well as verbs. According to that author, 'the Cajatambo accent is a fixed accent of tonal character, placed always and only on the first syllable of the word' (Carreño 2010: 54). … [Carreño:] The most curious thing is its phonetic realisation; it is a tonal accent, consisting of a slight rise in the pitch of the voice that accompanies the beginning of every word. That continuous succession of pitch rises, found in every Quechua phrase … [is what gives the language its characteristic 'sing-song']
tone_statements.locator: p. 93 (sec. 4 'A modo de conclusiones', running text + block quotation of Carreño 2010: 54; ex. (5) with tone letters on p. 94)

sources.note: This work describes Quechua dialects in general (family-wide survey); Cajatambo appears only as a name in the reproduced classifications of Torero 1964 (Huayhuash Occidental / Medio, printed p. 118) and Parker 1969/1971 (printed pp. 127-128, 130). sources.citation: Parker, Gary J. 1976. Gramática quechua: Ancash-Huailas. Lima: Ministerio de Educación / IEP, sec. 2.4 'Acentuación', pp.57-60.
sources.note: Describes Ancash: penultimate in most of Ancash; in Callejón de Huaylas clause-final words stress the non-final long syllable, else the initial syllable; clause-medial words stress the initial. Does not mention Cajatambo (checked by a full-text search for stress/accent) — it is the Ancash analogue Adelaar and Cerrón-Palomino pair with Cajatambo.

sources.note: Not a tone work: a 46-leaf CILA working paper on the origin of vowel quantity (long vs short vowels) in Quechua (LOC subjects: Vowels; Quantity). The only Cajatambo content seen is the Google Books snippet that lists 'quechua de Cajatambo (Lima)' with Huaral, Pasco and Junin (Tarma, Yauli) Quechua as one dialect group before describing 'la fonología de este grupo'. It may bear on syllable weight (the factor Torero/Cerrón-Palomino give for Cajatambo accent placement) but says nothing known about tone or pitch.

sources.note: Known only second-hand (Valqui 2018: 81-82, 91-93, table p. 96): first-hand phonology (108-leaf UNMSM licenciatura thesis by Edith Pineda Bernuy) of Huancapón (Cajatambo province) Quechua, Quechua I; its accent section (pp. 41, 46 cited) reports primary accent mostly on the first syllable of di- and trisyllables with a secondary accent in trisyllables ([á.Xa.lìn], [sár.si.yò:]), plural -kuna 'mantiene su propio acento, que viene a ser secundario' (p. 41), few trisyllables with penultimate accent except when the penult is CVC ([sa.kál.wa]), regular penultimate accent in four-syllable words, an…
